text: Henry Franklin "Buster" Smith (August 24, 1904 – August 10, 1991), also known as Professor Smith, was an American jazz alto saxophonist and mentor to Charlie Parker. He played a key role in developing the Texas Sax Sound while working with Count Basie and Lester Young in the 1930s. Smith performed with several prominent band leaders, including Duke Ellington, Earl Hines, and vocalist Ella Fitzgerald. He recorded his only album as leader in 1959, titled *The Legendary Buster Smith*, released by Atlantic Records, which featured songs such as "Kansas City Riffs," "Buster's Tune," "E Flat Boogie," and Kurt Weill's "September Song." For the sessions, he enlisted his brother Boston Smith to play piano and included musicians from throughout his career. Despite intending to record a follow-up, Smith was injured in an auto accident in the 1960s, which ended his ability to play the saxophone. He then began playing bass guitar in Dallas and continued to participate in the local music scene, leading a dance music band until 1980 and performing in the Legendary Revelations in the mid-1980s. Smith was born and raised in Alsdorf, Texas, a small township near Telico in the outskirts of Dallas, where he attended school as a child. He earned the nickname "Buster" from his parents due to being born as an overweight child; he was the third of five boys with no sisters, and both of his older brothers died in childhood from measles. His early musical influences were his mother and father, who played guitar; at age four, he played the organ with his brother, Boston Smith, who played the piano. His grandfather later gave away the family organ, believing it would lead Buster toward a life of sin. In 1919, Smith picked cotton for a week to earn $3.50 to buy a clarinet. By age eighteen, he had learned to play several instruments. In 1922, his family moved to Dallas, where he joined the Voodie White Trio, playing alto saxophone and clarinet. In 1923, he began his professional music career playing alto saxophone with medicine shows, where he had to play loudly to attract customers—an experience that shaped his loud musical style. In 1925, Oran "Hot Lips" Page invited him to join the Oklahoma City Blue Devils, where he wrote much of the group's music, learning from banjo player Johnny Clark and writing lyrics with co-workers from the bank. The Blue Devils' lineup included Walter Page, Oran Page, Lester Young, Count Basie, Jimmy Rushing, and Emir "Bucket" Coleman. They toured the Kansas City area and the Midwest, playing jazz for a year and bringing all members into prominence. Basie and Page left the group, but Smith stayed briefly before leaving as well. After leaving, he and Basie formed the Buster Smith-Count Basie Band of Rhythm, where they developed a louder style of jazz. Smith achieved a louder sound by using a tenor saxophone reed in his alto saxophone, and Lester Young complemented this by using a baritone saxophone reed on his tenor saxophone, a combination later known as the Texas Sax Sound. Smith gained significant influence in the Texan music community and mentored Charlie Parker during the 1930s, forming a "father-son relationship" through mentorship. In 1941, Smith returned to Dallas and stopped touring, remaining active in the local music scene. He wrote for jazz and blues bands, performed frequently, and taught young Texan musicians such as Aaron "T-Bone" Walker and Red Garland. He also performed session work with artists including Pete Johnson's Boogie-Woogie Boys, Eddie Durham, Leo "Snub" Mosley, Bon and His Buddies, and the Don Redman Orchestra. Smith died in Dallas on August 10, 1991, from a heart attack.
